project.title: Stepwise CAPE/CIN
project.summary: Designed and contributed an inflow layer visualization to the SounderPy sounding plot package.
project.content:
Designed and contributed a stepwise CAPE/CIN inflow layer visualization to [SounderPy](https://github.com/kylejgillett/sounderpy), a Python package used to generate sounding plots for meteorology research papers. The visualization helps determine whether an environment is likely to produce surface-based or elevated thunderstorms.

## Motivation

Soundings are usually summarized with single values such as SBCAPE and MUCAPE, which can hide where a storm's inflow actually comes from. I proposed [showing CAPE and CIN at every level of the atmosphere](https://bsky.app/profile/ryanvandersmith.com/post/3ldkhf2f5fs2u) so that tornadic, "mothership," and large-hail environments can be recognized at a glance.

The plot is a way to visualize the effective inflow layer (EIL), the lowest contiguous layer of air that can feed a storm's updraft. Operational tools approximate it with a single layer, which can be misleading in elevated environments where inflow comes from one or more layers above the surface.

## What it shows

- **Surface-based and tornadic:** a thick layer of uninhibited inflow near the surface, such as the 0-2 km layer in the 2024 Greenfield tornado environment, which is highly favorable for tornadoes.
- **Elevated:** inflow comes from layers above the surface, as in a sounding that produced 2.5" hail. Small amounts of CAPE can even exist above 6 km.
- **Large CAPE with large surface CIN:** often associated with photogenic, laminar "mothership" supercells. The stable air tends to keep tornadoes from forming, and these storms often start elevated before tapping lower-level CAPE.

## Pull requests

### Original inflow plot

[Pull request #33](https://github.com/kylejgillett/sounderpy/pull/33) added an opt-in `show_inflow` option to `build_sounding()`, drawing CAPE, 3CAPE, and CIN at each level on the skew-T. It added about 1-2% to the runtime of `build_sounding()`.

2023 Akron, CO supercell, which produced 27 tornadoes:

![Inflow plot for the 2023 Akron, CO supercell](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/afebaac9-c004-4332-a643-7e5c0407e9dc)

2024 messy MCS and tornado bust near Lufkin, TX, with a secondary inflow layer from 700-500 mb:

![Inflow plot near Lufkin, TX](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c4435c09-c6ba-4d2f-b780-8ddf79552945)

2024 Shreveport, LA tornado associated with Hurricane Beryl:

![Inflow plot for the Shreveport, LA tornado](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/882bdad0-7550-4a62-9d4e-a024bd7dfb43)

2024 Bedford, TX 2" hail event (elevated inflow):

![Inflow plot for the Bedford, TX hail event](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/dc14e116-ef0d-4e18-a528-b3b8ec4f4f7f)

### Merged version

SounderPy's maintainer, Kyle Gillett, suggested moving the visualization into the 0-3 km vertical plots at the bottom right of the sounding, next to the kinematics, to show what a storm is actually "feeling." [Pull request #34](https://github.com/kylejgillett/sounderpy/pull/34) replaced the "Theta & Theta-e" plot with "CIN & 3CAPE" and kept the original plot available behind a `show_theta` flag for backwards compatibility.

Compared with #33, it reduces information overload on the skew-T and is better for low-level storm behavior, at the cost of no longer showing mid- and upper-level convection.

Tornadic supercells:

![CIN and 3CAPE plot for tornadic supercells](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ee08e0be-4393-4ff1-94cd-f0f1f02276bc)

Elevated supercells:

![CIN and 3CAPE plot for elevated supercells](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/24d8e3ba-548a-4319-ae91-fea27a7b7608)

In-between cases (almost or slightly surface-based):

![CIN and 3CAPE plot for in-between cases](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c8584225-d12d-4c3e-84cb-4efd45d7374f)

Kyle then refined the design with fixed axis limits (CIN down to -300 J/kg, CAPE up to 2100 J/kg) and plotted CAPE instead of 3CAPE, so that soundings can be compared directly. Because anything above about 2000 J/kg indicates severity rather than inflow structure, this range works as a cutoff. The reworked version was merged in [pull request #35](https://github.com/kylejgillett/sounderpy/pull/35).

![Final plot with fixed CIN and CAPE axis limits](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/547f701b-a2da-4146-b00e-f698f7f6e747)

## Links

- [Bluesky thread with examples](https://bsky.app/profile/ryanvandersmith.com/post/3ldkhf2f5fs2u)
- [Effective inflow layer research (Monthly Weather Review)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/mwre/148/8/mwrD200013.xml)

profile.name: Ryan Vandersmith
profile.tagline: R&D software engineer building forecasting, visualization, and analysis tools for meteorology and atmospheric science.
profile.summary: Ryan Vandersmith is an R&D software engineer with over 10 years of experience and a deep self-taught background in meteorology. He builds weather forecasting and analysis tools used by photographers, storm chasers, and researchers, including Mesoview (skychaser.mesoview.app), a cloud inversion forecast tool, a mountain wave visualization tool, and a stepwise CAPE/CIN contribution to SounderPy. Professionally, he worked on Caffeine.ai, an AI website builder, and led Motoko programming-language tooling, including a VS Code extension with more than 85,000 installs. He also has experience with cross-chain EVM integrations, developer-experience products, UX research, Rust research software at the University of Colorado Boulder, consulting, and public-sector software.
expertise: weather forecasting and atmospheric analysis tools
MetPy, Siphon, Xarray, NumPy, and Pandas
